title: Deep Blue
why: IBM's Deep Blue, built by Feng-hsiung Hsu and Murray Campbell, beats Garry Kasparov, the first computer to win a match against a reigning world champion.

title: AlexNet
why: AlexNet, a neural net built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, identifies objects in photos far better than anything before it, starting the deep learning era.

title: AlphaGo
why: DeepMind's AlphaGo, led by David Silver and Aja Huang, beats Lee Sedol at Go, the hardest board game, a decade before experts expected.

title: Poker
why: Carnegie Mellon's Libratus, built by Tuomas Sandholm and Noam Brown, beats four of the world's best professionals at no-limit Texas hold'em, a game of hidden cards and bluffing.

title: AlphaZero
why: AlphaZero, built at DeepMind by David Silver, Thomas Hubert and Julian Schrittwieser, learns chess from scratch in hours, then beats Stockfish, the strongest chess engine.

title: Protein structure prediction
why: DeepMind's AlphaFold, led by Andrew Senior, predicts the 3D shapes of proteins better than every other team in the field's main contest.

title: Halicin
why: A neural network built by Jonathan Stokes, Regina Barzilay and James Collins at MIT discovers halicin, a new antibiotic that kills bacteria resistant to existing drugs.

title: Protein folding
why: AlphaFold 2, led by John Jumper and Demis Hassabis, predicts a protein's shape from its sequence as accurately as lab experiments, cracking a 50-year-old problem in biology and earning them a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Human protein structures
why: AlphaFold predicts the shapes of nearly every protein in the human body and releases them free to every scientist.

title: Knot theory
org: DeepMind, University of Oxford and University of Sydney
why: DeepMind's machine learning spots hidden patterns that lead mathematicians Marc Lackenby, András Juhász and Geordie Williamson to a new theorem about knots and a new approach to a 40-year-old conjecture about permutations.

title: Fusion plasma control
why: A neural network steers the superheated plasma inside a fusion reactor, a step toward fusion power.

title: Matrix multiplication
why: DeepMind's AlphaTensor, conceived by Alhussein Fawzi, finds ways to multiply grids of numbers in fewer steps, beating a record that stood for 50 years.

title: Sorting algorithms
why: Google DeepMind's AlphaDev, led by Daniel Mankowitz, finds faster ways to sort short lists that were added to the standard C++ library, the first change to that part of it in over a decade.

title: Herculaneum scrolls
org: Vesuvius Challenge and University of Kentucky
why: Machine-learning models built by students Luke Farritor and Youssef Nader read the first word, "purple," from inside a Herculaneum scroll charred shut by Vesuvius in 79 AD.

title: Weather forecasting
why: Google DeepMind's GraphCast forecasts the weather ten days out more accurately than the world's leading system, in under a minute.

title: New materials
why: Google DeepMind's GNoME, led by Ekin Dogus Cubuk and Amil Merchant, finds 2.2 million new crystals, 380,000 of them stable, about 800 years of discovery at the old pace.

title: Cap set problem
why: In work by Bernardino Romera-Paredes and Alhussein Fawzi with mathematician Jordan Ellenberg, DeepMind's FunSearch finds new answers to the cap set problem, an open question in math, the first time a language model has done so.

title: MRSA antibiotics
why: MIT's deep-learning models, in work led by Felix Wong and James Collins, find a new class of antibiotics that kills drug-resistant MRSA in mice and show which parts of the molecules do the work.

title: Drug binding
why: AlphaFold 3 predicts how proteins, DNA and drug molecules bind to each other, which is how most drugs work.

title: 4×4 matrix multiplication
why: Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve finds a faster way to multiply 4×4 grids of numbers than the method used since 1969.

title: Math Olympiad gold
why: Models from OpenAI and Google DeepMind score gold at the International Math Olympiad, the hardest math contest for students.

title: Gonorrhea antibiotics
why: A generative model built by Aarti Krishnan and James Collins at MIT designs two antibiotics from scratch, NG1 and DN1, which clear drug-resistant gonorrhea and MRSA infections in mice.

title: Phage genomes
why: The Evo genome models, run by Samuel King and Brian Hie at the Arc Institute, write whole genomes from scratch that boot up into 16 working bacteriophages, the first complete genomes designed by AI.

title: Hurricane Melissa
why: Google DeepMind's WeatherNext gives National Hurricane Center forecasters, with Philippe Papin on shift, the confidence to say three days ahead that Melissa, then a Category 1, would strike Jamaica as a Category 5, the first forecast that far up the scale.

title: Erdős unit distance conjecture
why: An OpenAI model run by Lijie Chen, with the proof checked by Mark Sellke and Mehtaab Sawhney, shows that points can have more pairs exactly one unit apart than Erdős conjectured 80 years ago.

title: Cycle double cover conjecture
why: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra proves this 50-year-old conjecture about networks in under an hour; mathematicians at TU Freiberg check the proof by computer.

title: Jacobian conjecture
why: Working with Claude on a question from Akhil Mathew, mathematician Levent Alpöge finds a one-line counterexample to an 87-year-old conjecture.

title: Ten open math problems
why: OpenAI's Astra settles or makes major progress on ten long-open problems at once, including showing that some infinite groups can't be approximated by finite ones.

title: Riemann zeros
why: Guided by Anthropic's Jarred Sumner, Claude raises the share of zeros proven to follow the Riemann hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%, a record decades of human work had barely moved.

title: Navier–Stokes problem
why: About 10,000 OpenAI agents produce a computer-checked proof that the equations of fluid flow can break down when a smooth force pushes the fluid, solving a Millennium Prize problem.

title: CRISPR-like system
why: Claude agents comb 200,000 enzymes that copy RNA into DNA and spot a CRISPR-like array of repeats beside one that no one had noticed, in work by Anthropic scientists Nicholas Perry and Matthew Durrant.

title: 3SUM and APSP hypotheses
why: An internal Claude model finds an algorithm, written up by Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams, that beats the textbook methods for 3SUM and all-pairs shortest paths, refuting two assumptions much of theoretical computer science was built on.

title: Quasi-Riemann hypothesis
why: OpenAI's models prove a weaker form of the Riemann hypothesis that Fields Medalist James Maynard called the best headline result in his field in 100 years, one of 722 papers OpenAI released in a single day.

title: Yang–Mills existence
why: OpenAI's models prove that the theory of gluons, the particles that carry the strong nuclear force, exists mathematically, half of a Millennium Prize problem; a panel led by Nobel laureate David Gross confirms the proof.

title: Kakeya conjecture
why: OpenAI's models settle the Kakeya conjecture in every dimension, proving that a set holding a needle pointing in every direction, though it can have zero volume, must still be full-dimensional.

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
why: OpenAI's models show that a core assumption behind hundreds of computer science papers is false, so some hard problems can be solved faster than anyone thought possible.

title: Hawking–Page transition
why: Claude Fable 5.2 finishes a calculation physicists set up in 2003 and never completed, showing that the switch from hot gas to black hole stays abrupt even where spacetime has no definite shape.

title: Riemann hypothesis
why: Working with Claude, mathematician Levent Alpöge proves the most famous open problem in math, posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.

title: Matrix multiplication exponent
why: OpenAI proves that the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4, matching the upper bound it found in October to settle a question open since 1969.
